_note: Second reading of AI reader 111's anchors (the day after: stimulants, MDMA, methylphenidate and DXM, 8 PMC papers).

tasks.page: Results › Effects of interventions; Data and analyses, Comparison 1
tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › (3) Average score in withdrawal symptoms and (4) Average score in craving; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 3, 3.1, 3.2 and 4
tasks.extracted: Withdrawal symptoms, two trials (Srisurapanont 1999b, Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire; Cruickshank 2008, Amphetamine Cessation Symptoms Assessment), 74 participants: SMD -0.08 (95% CI -0.54 to 0.38), no difference from placebo; amineptine -0.26 (-0.86 to 0.34), mirtazapine 0.17 (-0.54 to 0.89). Craving, one amineptine trial (Jittiwutikan 1997), 29 participants: MD 0.43 (-1.23 to 2.09), not significant. Kongsakon 2005 reported fewer withdrawal symptoms with mirtazapine as medians that could not be pooled.

tasks.page: Results › Effects of interventions; Data and analyses, Comparison 1
tasks.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › (1) Discontinuation rate and (2) Average score in global state; Data and analyses, Comparison 1, outcomes 1, 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2
tasks.extracted: Dropping out, four trials, 125 participants: any medicine RR 0.52 (0.29 to 0.94), I2 45%; amineptine RR 0.21 (0.07 to 0.69), two trials, 74; mirtazapine RR 0.98 (0.49 to 1.97), two trials, 51. Global state: amineptine MD -0.49 (-0.80 to -0.17), two trials, 72 (Clinical Global Impression); mirtazapine MD 0.30 (-0.22 to 0.82), one trial, 31 (BSI Global Severity Index); Kongsakon 2005 gave no global-state data.

tasks.page: Results › Risk of bias in included studies; Characteristics of included studies
tasks.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Allocation; Blinding; Characteristics of included studies, risk-of-bias tables; Results › Treatment regimes
tasks.extracted: Review's own judgments: allocation concealment low risk in 1 of 4 trials and unclear in 3; blinding for subjective outcomes (global state, craving, withdrawal symptoms) low risk in 1 and unclear in 3. The two amineptine trials, both from one Thai group, allowed occasional lorazepam for anxiety or insomnia. Adverse events, a planned primary outcome, are not reported for any trial.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice
tasks.extracted: The authors conclude that no available medicine has been shown to relieve amphetamine withdrawal: amineptine had limited benefits on drop-out and global state but none on withdrawal symptoms or craving and was withdrawn from the market in 1999 over reports of misuse; mirtazapine has not been shown to be effective, with few trials.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend (left panels, n = 6)
tasks.extracted: Actigraphy in 6 participants: total sleep after the highest dose 4.4 hours against 6.4 hours after placebo, an average reduction of 2 hours (p < .01); awakenings more frequent after the highest dose than after any other condition (p < .01).

tasks.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, sleep questionnaire rows
tasks.extracted: All 11 participants: estimated hours slept 7.70 (SEM 0.31) after placebo against 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the two higher doses, about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less (p < .001); 'fell asleep easily' 57.50 against 27.40 and 10.22; 'slept well' 85.20 against 49.60 and 21.44; 'woke often' 16.50 against 64.80 and 67.56; 'satisfied with sleep' 80.30 against 42.40 and 25.33 (df 1 and 30).

tasks.locator: 2.3 Sleep Monitoring; Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Actigraphy data were lost for the first five participants through equipment malfunction, so objective sleep comes from 6 of 11. The authors contrast nearly 5 fewer self-reported hours with 2 fewer measured hours and note that only single doses were studied, while use in daily life often involves repeated doses over consecutive days.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.2 Subjective effects; Table 1, subjective-effect rows
tasks.extracted: Next morning after the highest dose, against placebo: alert 38.09 against 55.55, content 37.36 against 53.91, friendly 43.00 against 65.00, social 40.82 against 67.09, talkative 37.36 against 58.46 (marked p < .05); energetic 22.80 against 35.20 marked only as different from the lowest dose; 'social' also lower after the lowest dose (50.36; F = 4.46).

tasks.locator: Results › 3.4 Physiological measures; Table 1, physiological rows
tasks.extracted: Next morning after the highest dose: heart rate 90.46 against 78.36 bpm, systolic pressure 124.00 against 118.00 and diastolic 78.55 against 69.00 mm Hg (all p < .05 against placebo); plasma methamphetamine still measurable after all three active doses.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.3 Cognitive/Psychomotor effects; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: No significant residual effect on the digit-symbol, repeated-acquisition, divided-attention, rapid-information and digit-recall tasks (no means or statistics given); ratings of 'depressed', 'anxious' and 'I want meth' were not altered by the previous day's dose (no values given).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors note that mood and performance were measured at only one morning time point, that subtle performance effects might need repeated testing through the day, that only single doses were studied, and that the persisting cardiovascular elevation may matter for toxicity with repeated use.

tasks.page: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms
tasks.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Treatment by time effects: depression beta -0.63, P = 0.001, end-of-programme BDI 2.43 (SD 4.22) with exercise against 4.82 (SD 5.71) with health education; anxiety beta -0.95, P = 0.001, BAI 2.18 (SD 4.94) against 5.11 (SD 7.79); adjusted for demographics.

tasks.page: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms
tasks.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph; Results › Participant characteristics
tasks.extracted: Baseline BDI 13.7 (SD 5.3) against 12.0 (SD 6.3), reported P = 0.21; baseline BAI 16.5 (SD 6.0) against 11.9 (SD 5.1), reported P = 0.08, with 69 and 66 randomized (editors' calculation: anxiety t about 4.8, p < 0.0001; depression p about 0.09). No harms or unintended effects in either group.

tasks.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01103531, Study Plan › Design Details; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures
tasks.extracted: Registered primary outcome: self-reported days of methamphetamine use over the 12 weeks after discharge; psychiatric symptoms registered as a secondary outcome measured to discharge and at 12 and 26 weeks after discharge; masking: none (open label). The paper calls depression and anxiety its primary outcomes and reports only the programme period.

tasks.locator: Methods › Statistical Analyses; Discussion, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The trial was powered to detect a 3.5-point difference (SD 5) between groups; the authors' limitations are a residential treatment sample, self-reported measures only, stress topics in the health-education sessions and a 70% male sample.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.1 Negative emotions, 3rd paragraph; Table 1, rows (16), (22), (23), (24); Discussion, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: A systematic review (17 entries) reports improved depression and anxiety with exercise in four entries: a 60-person trial (ref 16), two reports of the trial above (refs 22, 23) and a single dance session in women (ref 24); no numbers, no appraisal, and the trial above is counted three times across the review.

tasks.locator: Results › 3.3 Drug cravings, 3rd paragraph; Table 1, rows (25), (30), (34), (35), (36), (37); Discussion, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Lower craving reported with single sessions of dance or aerobic exercise in women (ref 34), acute cycling (ref 30), acute exercise compared across intensities (ref 25), a programme of aerobic and resistance exercise with lower inflammatory markers (ref 35) and Tai Chi in women (ref 36); less methamphetamine use after the programme among people with lower-severity use (ref 37). No numbers given.

tasks.locator: 2. Methodology, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1, rows (22), (23), (29), (37)
tasks.extracted: Search of two databases, English only, 2014 to 2023; risk of bias said to be assessed with AMSTAR 2 (a tool for reviews) with no results reported; no additional data requested and no analysis beyond the articles. One 135-person trial appears three times and one entry is a protocol without results.

tasks.locator: Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend
tasks.extracted: Main effects of abstinence week on every polysomnographic measure (for example sleep latency F(2,36) = 20.0, p < 0.0001; total sleep F(2,36) = 4.1, p = 0.025); week 1 to week 3: sleep onset latency t(36) = -4.9 (p < 0.0001), slow-wave sleep t(36) = -3.5 (p = 0.001) and REM latency t(36) = -4.0 (p = 0.0003) increased, total sleep t(36) = 2.8 (p = 0.008) and REM time t(36) = 3.0 (p = 0.005) decreased.

tasks.page: Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures
tasks.locator: Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Self-rated sleep and alertness improved over abstinence: overall sleep quality F(2,36) = 9.0 (p = 0.0007), depth 6.3 (p = 0.0044), feeling rested 5.9 (p = 0.0063), alertness on waking 8.3 (p = 0.0011), daytime alertness 7.2 (p = 0.0023); no modafinil effect on these ratings (all p > 0.35).

tasks.locator: Results › Comparisons to Controls; Figure 3 legend
tasks.extracted: At week 3 against 12 healthy men: group differences in slow-wave sleep (F(2,29) = 4.9, p = 0.015), REM time (3.5, p = 0.04), total sleep (12.1, p < 0.0001) and sleep onset latency (4.7, p = 0.017); post hoc, REM time was lower and sleep latency longer in the placebo group (not the modafinil group) than in the healthy men; self-rated sleep quality did not differ (77, 81 and 67; p = 0.16).

tasks.locator: Methods › Healthy Comparison Participants; Discussion, 2nd and 7th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The healthy men lived outside the unit, took no capsule and were recorded on a single night after one adaptation night; the authors name the fixed bedtime, uncontrolled daytime light, few non-treatment-seeking participants and possible withdrawal from other substances as limitations, and say the findings reproduce their 2006 study.

tasks.locator: Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Main effects of modafinil on sleep onset latency (F(1,18) = 5.8, p = 0.027) and slow-wave sleep (F(1,18) = 11.9, p = 0.0029; more than double the placebo value at all time points per the Discussion); drug by week interactions for total sleep (F(2,36) = 7.4, p = 0.0021) with longer total sleep (F(1,36) = 6.7, p = 0.013) and shorter REM latency (F(1,36) = 6.9, p = 0.013) at week 3; no REM-time difference at any week (all p > 0.17).

tasks.page: Results › Multiple Sleep Latency Tests; Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures
tasks.locator: Results › Multiple Sleep Latency Tests; Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2 legend
tasks.extracted: Nap-test sleep latency longer with modafinil in week 1 only (15, SEM 2, against 10, SEM 2, minutes; F(1,36) = 4.4, p = 0.04); sleepiness ratings lower with modafinil at the morning ratings and the afternoon ratings in weeks 2 and 3 (three-way interaction F(4,144) = 2.7, p = 0.036), not at the evening rating; no effect on self-rated sleep quality, depth, restedness or alertness (all p > 0.35).

tasks.locator: Results › Adverse Events
tasks.extracted: Eight participants (6 on modafinil, 2 on placebo) had 9 adverse events: headache 4 against 1, nausea without vomiting 2 against 0, palpitations in 1 on modafinil (evaluated in the emergency department; dose temporarily reduced), conjunctivitis in 1 on placebo; the others mild.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors state that the sample was small for a placebo-controlled study and was powered only to detect the previously observed changes in sleep over abstinence within each group; they also note the lack of occipital EEG leads, the fixed bedtime and the uncontrolled daytime light.

tasks.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: 35 trials, 75 observations, 3079 patients on methylphenidate and 2606 on placebo; pooled relative risks insomnia 1.61 (z = 9.2), initial insomnia 2.78 (z = 6.6), middle insomnia 2.97 (z printed as 183), combined insomnia 2.97 (z = 6.4), sleep disorder 1.99 (z = 4.2), all p < 0.001.

tasks.page: Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders; Figure 2
tasks.locator: Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
tasks.extracted: Adjusted relative risks for insomnia in individual trials ranged widely: more than 75% not significantly different from 1, some significantly below 1 and some above 1; Egger's test t = 0.37, p = 0.7.

tasks.page: Results › The Impact of Placebo AE Rates on the RR Statistic; Discussion
tasks.locator: Results › The Impact of Placebo AE Rates on the RR Statistic; Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Drug and placebo adverse-event rates were highly correlated (r = 0.89, p < 0.0001) and observed relative risks were close to those predicted from the placebo rate alone; eliciting adverse events with questionnaires gives higher absolute rates but smaller relative risks than spontaneous reporting, so relative risks should be read with absolute risks, which the review does not report in its text.

tasks.locator: Acknowledgements; Authors' Disclosures
tasks.extracted: Manuscript development funded by Ironshore Pharmaceuticals, whose product is among those compared; two Ironshore employees assisted with data extraction and two authors are employees of its parent company, Highland Therapeutics.

tasks.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3, treatment column
tasks.extracted: MDMA against placebo (df 1 and 6): total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes, F = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, F = 7.0, P = 0.038; stage 1 8.4 against 6.6%, F = 9.49, P = 0.022; REM 3.5 (2.1) against 19.2 (2.0)%, F = 14.28, P = 0.009, reduced on the treatment night only (interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003); no effect on wake after sleep onset, stage 2 (P = 0.267), stage 3/4 (P = 0.119) or REM latency (P = 0.589).

tasks.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Table 3
tasks.extracted: On the treatment night, REM percentage after MDMA was lower than after both shortened sleep (19.3%; P = 0.004) and placebo (P = 0.004) (F(2,12) = 15.036), which the authors read as a specific REM-suppressing effect beyond sleep loss.

tasks.locator: Table 3, recovery column; Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Recovery night with placebo after the MDMA session: total sleep 403.6 (SEM 34.4) minutes and REM 22.2% (1.5), against 431.9 minutes and 20.6% on the recovery night of the placebo session; no main effects of night apart from the REM interaction.

tasks.locator: Methods › Experimental Procedures, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 9th paragraph; Abstract › Measurements and Results
tasks.extracted: Only 7 completed; two withdrew and the 12-sequence Latin square was incomplete; the laboratory schedule was earlier than the participants' usual sleep times. The abstract states that MDMA reduced stage 3/4 sleep, which the drug comparison does not show (P = 0.119).

tasks.page: Results › Effects on the MSLT; Figure 4
tasks.locator: Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Treatment by day interaction F = 4.63 (df 2 and 12), P = 0.032; after shortened sleep the mean nap-test latency was shorter than after placebo (about 6 minutes, per the Discussion), while after MDMA it differed neither from placebo nor from shortened sleep; no differences on the day after the recovery night; sleep-onset REM periods 2.14 (shortened sleep), 1.43 (MDMA), 1.00 (placebo), not significant.

tasks.locator: Abstract › Measurements and Results and Conclusions; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors conclude that MDMA's sleep loss was not associated with next-day sleepiness and that next-day sleep latency remained at placebo levels; with 7 participants, MDMA's next-day values were not significantly different from those after shortened sleep either.

tasks.page: Results › Time-course of drug effects; Figure 1
tasks.locator: Results › Time-course of drug effects; Figure 1 legend
tasks.extracted: Effects generally significant by the first post-dose test, maximal over the following tests and decreasing at the last; DXM produced longer-lasting Balance and Circular Lights deficits than triazolam; at the penultimate and maximum DXM doses, deficits were still apparent at the last assessment; the highest doses sometimes produced complete impairment (scored 0).

tasks.locator: Results › Emesis
tasks.extracted: No vomiting after placebo, triazolam or the two lowest DXM doses; 2 of 12 vomited at the third dose level and 7 of 12 at the fourth level or above; vomiting at one dose did not always predict vomiting at the next.

tasks.page: Abstract; Materials and Methods › General Procedures
tasks.locator: Abstract › Results; Materials and Methods › General Procedures, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The abstract states that drug effects resolved without significant adverse effects by the end of the session; the end-of-session measures, taken when acute effects were judged to have resolved, were questionnaires, and psychomotor tasks were last given at the final in-session test.

tasks.page: Materials and Methods › General Procedures; Data Analysis
tasks.locator: Materials and Methods › General Procedures, 5th paragraph; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Doses within each drug always rose and escalation stopped when a person could not complete a psychomotor and a computer task, or when the participant or investigator judged a higher dose inadvisable; data were missing at stop-point sessions.

tasks.page: Results › Measures assessed 1 month after drug administration › Persisting Effects Questionnaire
tasks.locator: Results › Measures assessed 1 month after drug administration › Persisting Effects Questionnaire, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: About one month after the final session: positive changes in attitudes about life and self, mood, social effects, behaviour and spirituality at 46% to 61% of maximum scores, negative ratings low; 4 of 12 rated the experiences among the five most meaningful of their lives and 7 of 12 among the five most spiritually significant; all 12 reported increased well-being (1 slightly, 7 moderately, 4 very much). The questionnaire could not separate DXM from triazolam sessions; in interviews, effects were attributed to sessions thought to be a classic hallucinogen.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: One participant reached a stop point after a post-session headache attributed to DXM; the primary monitor was reachable by phone throughout, no volunteer called or reported distress after the sessions, and no lasting distress or persisting perceptual phenomena were reported at the one-month follow-up.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph; Materials and Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors note that volunteers knew the laboratory's psilocybin research and may have expected psilocybin, and that preparation, social support and the setting may have shaped their positive ratings; people with a personal or immediate-family history of schizophrenia, bipolar, delusional, paranoid or schizoaffective disorder were excluded.
